The Story of the Plasterer's Vow

I bow to Lord Jina, whose feet are the cause of merit, and I write the story of one who attained the fruit through making a vow — "I shall not do such-and-such until this task is complete" — a story that brings happiness.

King Vasupal of Ahichchhatpur was very wise. He had great faith in Jain dharma. His queen was Vasumati, who was equally intelligent and devoted to dharma. Vasupal had built a very large and beautiful Jain temple called Sahasrakoot, in which he had installed an image of Lord Parshvanath.

The king called a skilled painter to apply plaster to the image. Following the royal order, the painter applied the plaster beautifully. But at night, the plaster fell off. The next day, the same thing happened. In short, he would apply plaster during the day and it would fall off at night. Many days passed this way. He could not understand why this was happening. He and the king were greatly distressed.

The truth was that the plasterer was a meat-eater. Therefore, because of his impurity, the plaster would not stay on the image. Then a monk gave the plasterer knowledge of this fact, saying, "This is a very special image. A guardian goddess or god is always appointed to protect it. Therefore, until this work is complete, you must take a vow not to eat meat."

The plasterer did exactly as the monk advised. He took the vow of not eating meat from the monk. Afterward, when he applied plaster the next day, this time it stayed. Truly, the work of those who observe vows is always accomplished. The king then honoured the painter with fine clothes and ornaments.

Just as this plasterer made a vow for the success of his work, so too should others and monks make vows (avgrah or pratima) in matters of spreading knowledge, propagating the faith, and other religious works.

May the knowledge taught by Lord Jinendra — the ocean of knowledge, which makes one omniscient, which is served by supremely pure monks for the attainment of the soul's happiness, and which is worshipped with devotion by gods, Vidyadharas, Chakravartins, and other great beings — may that knowledge make me too omniscient.

This story teaches that vows and self-discipline are essential for the success of any endeavour. The plasterer's impurity from eating meat prevented his work from succeeding, but when he took a vow to abstain, his work was accomplished. The wise should take appropriate vows to support their spiritual and worldly goals, for self-discipline is the foundation of all achievement.
